newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels suspend talks, allege attack planned.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels suspend talks, allege attack planned.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 72 VIP hostages abruptly broke off negotiations on Thursday alleging the government was secretly digging a tunnel to storm the Japanese ambassador's home.

Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa said he had evidence the government aimed to rescue the hostages while he and his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, attended talks at a safe house across the street from the diplomatic residence.
The meeting scheduled for Friday would have been the tenth round of talks in the 80-day hostage crisis.

"Tomorrow we are not going to attend the negotiations because the right conditions do not exist for a transparent process," the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader said in a walkie-talkie interview from within the residence.

"All of a sudden they are waiting for us to leave to start an attack, taking advantage of our absence," he said. "Without doubt (there is) a tactic to attack from the outside ... We have been hearing noises from underneath the floor of the house."

There was no official reaction from Peruvian police. But security force sources consulted by Reuters confirmed that at least four tunnels had been dug under the besieged compound in recent weeks while loud music was played by police outside.
The tunnels would be used if there was an attack, which would last seven minutes and cause many deaths, they added.
While President Alberto Fujimori and his chief negotiator Domingo Palermo withheld comment, Defence Minister Tomas Meza Castillo denied Cerpa's accusations during a visit to Bolivia.
"I believe that it is the result of the MRTA members' nervousness, nothing else," he told reporters in La Paz.
Palermo said the government was seeking a peaceful solution to the crisis and would only use "other methods" if any of the hostages was harmed.

The daily La Republica, in an early Friday edition, said its reporters had observed since mid-January that material was being brought out of a house on a street behind the residence between 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. every night.
Guards confirmed the material was earth that was driven away in police vehicles and dumped at a Lima beach and later at the National Intelligence Service headquarters, the newspaper added.
Cerpa said the rebels would not return to the negotiating table until the security situation "was cleared up" with the commission of guarantors overseeing talks.

Fujimori broke off a trip to the Andean province of Cuzco and returned to Lima without speaking to the press. He met Palermo met late on Thursday to discuss the latest twist in what is Latin America's longest hostage siege.

Representatives from the Red Cross, Vatican and Canadian government -- who form a three-man guarantor committee overseeing negotiations -- entered the residence to talk to Cerpa but left without comment.
Despite the accusation, police continued their policy of blaring loud music at the residence, playing traditional Peruvian music and children's tunes in the evening.
Analysts were sceptical of Cerpa's claim that security forces were digging tunnels to enter the residence.

"I do not think the government would engage in such a flagrant contradiction ... appearing to be seeking a peaceful end while it dug tunnels for a completely military solution," political analyst Enrique Bernales told a local radio station.
At the last round of talks on Wednesday the government presented the MRTA with what Fujimori called an "all-inclusive" proposal for a peaceful end to the siege.
This followed the MRTA's unenthusiastic reaction to Cuban President Fidel Castro's offer of asylum for the 20-odd guerrillas holding the residence.

The rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of cocktail party guests. They released most in the following weeks but still hold Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two government ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
